newsitem.title: UK: Unilever new chief to reshape giant empire.
newsitem.headline: Unilever new chief to reshape giant empire.

text.p: Unilever co-chairman Niall FitzGerald who took office at the Anglo-Dutch consumer products firm this week, is likely to spark a faster, more radical restructuring of the sprawling empire, analysts said on Tuesday.

Analysts said investors are banking on FitzGerald's leadership to spur sweeping change and to revive stagnant growth but they warned that longer-term benefits might be won at the cost of short-term pain.
"They may need to stomach some short term earnings dilution to boost returns in the long run," said one analyst who asked not to be identified.
Major restructuring plans were already under consideration, according to food industry analysts, but now investors are looking to FitzGerald to implement them more rapidly.
"People were anticipating his arrival would be a trigger for the restructuring to happen faster," said one industry analyst who asked not to be identified.

Investors see Fitzgerald, who at 50 is young for a Unilever chairman, bringing a change of culture at the traditionally conservative group. The company's recent performance has been sluggish and profits in this year's second quarter fell six percent to 616 million pounds ($961.6 million).
Unilever's vast size -- around 500 companies spanning 90 countries -- means revamping it is a mammoth task, which is unlikely to happen overnight.
The shake-up could involve selling off 20 percent of the group's total businesses with seven billion pounds in annual sales, analysts said.
There is speculation Unilever might even be willing to divest some major divisions which operate in mature markets or where Unilever does not have market leadership.

Some see dangers in Fitzgerald's appointment as he was in overall charge of Unilever's detergents business when its Persil Power soap powder lost out in a ruthless "soap war" with arch rival Procter & Gamble Co.
But proceeds from some major sell-offs would boost resources for Unilever's operations in emerging markets, where it has the edge over key rivals and greatest potential for growth.

Analysts see businesses in Europe as being high on the list of possible disposals. "There are a lot of underperforming businesses in Europe and a lot of the pruning is likely to be in Europe," said David Lang at Henderson Crosthwaite. Food companies which may be up for sale probably include John West, a UK fish business and Nordsee, a German frozen fish business.

Unilever's shares surged this week on reports of Fitzgerald's multi-billion pound restructuring plans but analysts said that realistically any major improvement in performance is a couple of years away.
If the restructuring does start to throw off cash then this could have implications for shareholder value, which Fitzgerald is emphasising, analysts said.
"The dividend payment ratio won't change at the moment, but it the company starts producting big cash surpluses then they will have to decide what to do with it," said Lang.
But in the meantime analysts are remaining cautious and want to wait for the evidence of change to come through.
"Unilever is an evolutionary business rather than a revolutionary one, but maybe we're in for a period of mild revolution," said John Campbell, European food analyst at Paribas Capital Markets.
